lessons.title: Multi-Threaded Task Offloading via Web Workers
lessons.description: Move heavy computation off the main thread using Web Workers — keep your UI responsive.

sections.heading: What are Web Workers?
paragraphs: Web Workers run JavaScript in a separate thread, keeping the main thread free for UI updates. They communicate with the main thread via messages.
list: Runs in a separate thread — doesn't block the UI
No access to the DOM — only communicates via messages

codeExamples.heading: Basic Web Worker
explanation: new Worker() creates a separate thread for the script.
postMessage() sends data to the worker.
The worker runs independently — the UI stays responsive.

practice.task: Offload a heavy computation (summing 10 million numbers) to a Web Worker. Compare the UI responsiveness with and without the worker.
hints: Create worker.js that sums the numbers.
Log the time taken and verify the UI stays responsive.

keyTakeaways: Web Workers run JavaScript in a separate thread — no UI blocking.
Communication happens via postMessage/onmessage — no shared state.
Workers have no DOM access — they're pure computation threads.
Perfect for heavy calculations, data processing and image manipulation.
lessons.challenge: Build a search engine that indexes documents using a Web Worker, keeping the UI responsive during indexing.

lessons.title: Message Passing & Structured Clone Algorithm
lessons.description: Data sent between workers is cloned using the structured clone algorithm — understand what can and can't be transferred.

sections.heading: Structured clone
list: Objects sent via postMessage are deep-cloned automatically
Supports: objects, arrays, Map, Set, Date, RegExp, Blob, ArrayBuffer
Does NOT support: functions, DOM nodes, class instances (loses prototype)
Transferable objects (ArrayBuffer) can be moved instead of cloned — zero-copy

codeExamples.heading: Structured clone and transferables
explanation: Structured clone creates a deep copy of complex objects.
Maps, Sets and Dates survive the clone — they're real instances.
Functions and DOM nodes cannot be cloned.
Transferable objects are moved (zero-copy) instead of cloned.

practice.task: Send a complex object with nested arrays and a Map to a Web Worker. Verify the worker receives a deep copy, not a reference.
hints: Create an object with nested structures and a Map.
In the worker, modify the data and verify the original is unchanged.

keyTakeaways: Structured clone creates deep copies of complex objects for postMessage.
Maps, Sets and Dates survive cloning; functions and DOM nodes don't.
Transferable objects (ArrayBuffer) are moved, not cloned — zero-copy.
Choose structured clone for complex data, transferables for large buffers.
lessons.challenge: Compare performance of structured clone vs transfer for a 10MB ArrayBuffer.

lessons.title: Shared Memory Access with SharedArrayBuffer & Atomics Operations
lessons.description: Share memory between workers for true parallel data access — use Atomics for synchronization.

sections.heading: SharedArrayBuffer
list: Both main thread and workers can read/write the same memory
Atomics API provides atomic operations for synchronization
Requires specific HTTP headers: Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy, Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy

codeExamples.heading: SharedArrayBuffer basics
explanation: SharedArrayBuffer allows multiple threads to access the same memory.
Atomics operations are thread-safe — they can't be interrupted.
Atomics.wait() blocks a thread until a condition is met.
Atomics.add() atomically increments a value — no race conditions.

practice.task: Create a SharedArrayBuffer that both the main thread and a worker can write to. Use Atomics to safely coordinate access.

keyTakeaways: SharedArrayBuffer enables true shared memory between threads.
Atomics API provides thread-safe operations: add, load, store, wait, notify.
Requires specific security headers for browser support.
Use SharedArrayBuffer for high-performance parallel computing.
lessons.challenge: Implement a parallel array sum using SharedArrayBuffer where multiple workers process different chunks simultaneously.
